name_en: Yunnan Gu Shu Bai Cha (Ancient Tree White)
processing: Withered and dried like other white teas, by sun, oven or shade. Nothing particular to old-tree material is well documented; the difference is mainly in the raw leaf.
harvest_season: Usually spring, as for most Yunnan white tea, though little is documented for old-tree lots specifically.
appearance_dry: Large, thick buds and leaves in dark green and silver, bigger than most Fujian white tea.
appearance_liquor: Clear pale gold to amber, typical of Yunnan white teas.
appearance_wet: Thick, large leaves and plump buds, soft and supple.
taste_profile: Sellers describe a refreshing aroma and a natural lingering sweetness; the Yunnan large-leaf material is typically fuller than Fujian white tea.

brewing.notes: General guidance for Yunnan white tea. Thicker leaf rewards hot water and many short rounds.

vintage_note: No single standard. Usual Yunnan practice is loose or pressed lots sold by harvest year, sometimes aged. Ancient-tree is not a regulated claim here and is easy to overstate, so ask for the mountain, the tree age and the year.
description:
Ancient-tree white tea is a market label more than a defined tea: white tea made from old Yunnan tea trees. Jinggu in Pu'er prefecture, which calls itself a century-old home of white tea, is a name often connected with Yunnan white tea.

The method is the same plain wither and dry used for other white teas. Yunnan large-leaf material brings its own weight, so expect more body than a Fujian white as a general rule.

Sellers talk about a refreshing aroma and a lingering sweet return. Hot water and short steeps show this kind of leaf best.

Be sceptical of the words ancient tree: nothing regulates them and the premium attracts loose claims. A seller who names a village or mountain and can tell you the tree age and year is worth more than one who only uses the phrase.
history: Little is documented about ancient-tree white tea as a named product. Jinggu promotes itself as a century-old white tea home. The name itself appears to be a modern selling term that became common along with the wider interest in Yunnan white tea.
